objective: Interpret Cilium network policies and their intent: endpointSelector, ingress and egress rules, and what a policy allows at L3, L4 and L7
secondaryObjectives: Policy enforcement modes: default, always and never, and what each means for endpoints with no policy
Write policy rules using the policy rule structure: CiliumNetworkPolicy and CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, toEndpoints, toFQDNs, toEntities, toCIDR, toPorts with L7 rules
Understand Cilium's identity-based network security model: security identities derived from labels, how they replace IP-based rules, and how identities are shared across nodes

Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of the page found by search. default enforces policy only on endpoints a rule selects (unselected endpoints are unrestricted); always enforces on all endpoints; never disables enforcement. A rule selecting an endpoint with an ingress or egress section makes that direction default-deny.

Found by search 2026-11-17 and read only through the search listing (title and address); to verify against the page. Used for: common Cilium policy mistakes, including a toFQDNs rule without a DNS rule that lets the DNS proxy see lookups.

The company, the clusters, the services and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the network engineer at Ledgerwise, a fictional fintech. An auditor asked that the payments namespace only talk to the card processor's API and its own database. A colleague applied a first CiliumNetworkPolicy ten minutes ago; since then every payment fails.
handover: The policy selects app=payments-api with one egress rule: toEndpoints app=payments-db on port 5432.
The card processor is reached as api.cardproc.example on port 443; its IP addresses change.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: with enforcement off, the internal admin namespace is reachable from the public web tier; the security team opens an incident.
Check-in 3: the auditor's scan shows payments-api can reach any internet address on any port; the control fails the audit.
Check-in 4: the database Pod is rescheduled during a node update; its IP changes and payments cannot reach it.

effects.log: Check-in 2: lookups work; calls to the processor are still dropped.
Check-in 3: a teammate wants to switch the database rule to the database's Pod IP.

dnsPrompt.title: Egress is default-deny now
dnsPrompt.context: Every lookup from payments-api is dropped.

choices.label: Add an egress rule to kube-dns on port 53 with an L7 DNS rule (matchPattern '*'), keeping the policy's default deny

effects.log: DNS is allowed through Cilium's DNS proxy.

choices.feedback: Selecting an endpoint makes its egress default-deny; DNS has to be allowed, and an L7 DNS rule lets later FQDN rules work.

choices.label: Allow UDP 53 to kube-dns without a DNS rule
choices.feedback: Lookups work, but without the L7 DNS rule Cilium cannot learn names, so a toFQDNs rule will not work.

choices.label: Set the policy enforcement mode to never cluster-wide until the policy is fixed

effects.log: Enforcement is off for the whole cluster.

choices.feedback: never disables enforcement everywhere: every other namespace's policies stop protecting it too.

fqdnPrompt.title: The processor's addresses change
fqdnPrompt.context: api.cardproc.example resolves to addresses that change several times a day.

choices.label: Add a toFQDNs rule for api.cardproc.example on port 443

effects.log: Egress is allowed to whatever the name resolves to.

choices.feedback: toFQDNs follows the name through the DNS proxy, so address changes need no policy change.

choices.label: Add a toCIDR rule for the three addresses the name resolves to now
choices.feedback: It works until the processor's addresses change, then payments fail again.

choices.label: Add toEntities: world on all ports

effects.log: payments-api may now reach anything outside the cluster.

choices.feedback: This undoes what the auditor asked for: payments can now reach any address on any port.

identPrompt.title: Labels or addresses for the database?
identPrompt.context: A teammate says the database rule 'feels fragile' and wants toCIDR on the database Pod's current IP.

choices.label: Keep toEndpoints on the database's labels: Cilium derives an identity from them and every node enforces it, whatever the Pod's IP
choices.feedback: Identities come from labels and are shared across nodes, so a rescheduled database keeps working.

choices.label: Add the Pod IP as a toCIDR rule alongside the label rule, just in case

effects.log: A redundant CIDR rule is added.

choices.feedback: Harmless today, but the CIDR rule will allow whatever Pod gets that IP next.

choices.label: Replace the label rule with toCIDR on the database Pod's current IP

effects.log: The label rule is replaced by today's IP.

choices.feedback: Pod IPs change on reschedule: the database moves and payments lose it.

scoring.modelReasoning: In Cilium's default enforcement mode an endpoint is unrestricted until a policy selects it; once a rule with an egress section selects it, egress is default-deny. So DNS must be allowed explicitly, and an L7 DNS rule lets the DNS proxy learn names for toFQDNs. External services with changing addresses are allowed by name on their port, not by today's CIDR and never by 'world'. In-cluster peers are selected by labels: Cilium turns labels into identities that every node enforces, whatever the Pod's IP.
